subject: Embedding space fragmentation in continual learning systems as a function of replay buffer diversity and task boundary sharpness

Topic: Embedding space fragmentation in continual learning systems as a function of replay buffer diversity and task boundary sharpness

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1885)
response:
Continual learning systems face a core tension: a neural network trained sequentially on tasks T₁, T₂, ... T_n must share a single embedding space across all tasks, yet gradient updates for T_n tend to overwrite representations that were useful for T₁—this is catastrophic forgetting. The central question here is whether that forgetting is uniform or structured: does the embedding space fracture into disconnected, task-specific clusters (fragmentation), does it collapse into an undifferentiated blur, or does something more geometrically complex happen depending on how diverse the replay buffer is and how abruptly task boundaries occur? Replay buffers—stored exemplars from prior tasks used to interleave old data during new training—are the standard mitigation, but their diversity (whether stored samples span the full distribution of a task or just its modes) determines whether they actually anchor the relevant regions of embedding space or merely prevent the most egregious overwriting. Task boundary sharpness matters because a hard boundary (one batch of T₁, then immediately T₂) produces a sharp gradient signal shift that can catastrophically reorganize representations, whereas gradual boundaries allow the optimizer to find smoother interpolations. What a beginner misses is that the problem isn't just accuracy degradation—it's that the geometry of the embedding space can become pathological in ways that don't show up in downstream task metrics until much later: two tasks may appear to perform acceptably while their representations have silently merged or orthogonalized in ways that make a third task's learning suddenly and mysteriously fail.

NEXT: When replay buffer diversity is held constant, what specific geometric signatures in the embedding space would you expect to differ between a system exposed to sharp task boundaries versus gradual ones—and how would you measure them?

With sharp task boundaries, the dominant geometric signature is subspace rotation: the principal components of task T₁'s representations get actively reoriented to serve T₂, rather than merely compressed. Nguyen et al. (2019) in the EWC follow-up literature and more precisely Ramasesh et al. (2021) showed that sharp boundaries produce high CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment) drops between pre- and post-switch representations of the same inputs—CKA falling from ~0.8 to ~0.4 in a single task transition is not unusual in networks without strong regularization. Gradual boundaries, by contrast, tend to produce intrinsic dimensionality expansion rather than rotation: the embedding cloud grows to accommodate new structure without forcibly displacing old structure, which you can track with two-NN estimators of intrinsic dimension (Facco et al., 2017) and typically see as a 20–40% dimensionality increase rather than a directional shift. A third signature is inter-task class distance collapse: under sharp boundaries, the average cosine distance between centroids of T₁ classes and T₂ classes in the shared space decreases faster than under gradual boundaries, because the optimizer is not penalized for reusing the same embedding directions. You measure these concretely by taking frozen probes at checkpoints—freeze the encoder, extract embeddings for held-out sets from all seen tasks, compute CKA across checkpoint pairs, estimate intrinsic dimension, and track centroid geometry—which gives you a task-by-time matrix of geometric health that separates forgetting-as-rotation from forgetting-as-collapse.

Orthogonal gradient projection (OGP), as formalized in Farajtabar et al. (2020) and refined in GPM (Saha et al., 2021), constrains new gradients to lie in the null space of the subspace spanned by prior task gradients—but this assumes that the gradient subspace and the representation subspace that matters for task performance are the same thing, and they aren't. The gradient subspace captures directions of high parameter sensitivity during training, while the functionally important representation subspace is defined by which directions in activation space downstream classifiers actually use—these can be substantially misaligned, especially in deeper layers where representations are highly nonlinear functions of parameters. GPM in practice needs to retain roughly 80–95% of the gradient subspace variance to prevent forgetting, which means the null space available for new learning shrinks rapidly with each task: Saha et al. report that by task 5 on Split-CIFAR, the projectable subspace has contracted enough that new task gradients are heavily distorted, producing a different failure mode—representation stagnation, where new tasks can't be learned well rather than old tasks being forgotten. What this reveals geometrically is that embedding space fragmentation isn't just about rotation or displacement of existing structure; it's also about rank exhaustion—the usable rank of the shared embedding space gets consumed by successive task subspaces, and OGP makes this consumption explicit and irreversible rather than implicit and partially recoverable via replay. The deeper reveal is that the geometry is not flat: the manifolds on which task-relevant representations live are curved, and linear subspace methods like OGP are approximating curved constraint surfaces with hyperplanes, so the error compounds across tasks in proportion to manifold curvature rather than task count alone.

Increasing width does buy real capacity, but with a deeply sublinear return: empirically, doubling width does not double the number of tasks you can learn without interference, because the effective rank actually used by any given task scales roughly as the square root of the nominal dimension in overparameterized networks—a finding consistent with the intrinsic dimensionality literature (Aghajanyan et al., 2021, showed that fine-tuning tasks on large LLMs occupy surprisingly low intrinsic dimensions, often 100–1000 dimensions regardless of ambient dimension in the millions). The core problem is that gradient descent in wide networks doesn't spread task representations evenly across available dimensions; it finds low-rank solutions preferentially due to the implicit regularization of SGD, so a 4x wider network might only give you 1.5–2x more usable orthogonal subspace per task. Cossu et al. (2021) and related PackNet-style ablations show that explicit capacity allocation—hard-masking subnetworks per task—scales more linearly with width than soft projection methods, precisely because it forces rank usage to be spread rather than concentrated. There's also a depth interaction that makes width scaling alone misleading: in deeper networks, the effective rank of representations tends to decrease through layers (a well-documented "rank collapse" phenomenon in transformers and deep ResNets), so adding width at shallow layers doesn't proportionally increase rank at the layer where task-discriminative representations actually form. The practical upshot is that width scaling is a slow, expensive solution to rank exhaustion—you're buying maybe 3–5 additional tasks of clean capacity for a 10x parameter increase, which is why the field has moved toward architectural solutions like dynamic expansion and sparse coding rather than brute-force scaling.

response:
Spectral regularization does preserve more orthogonal capacity—but the mechanism is more subtle than simply "keeping rank high." Kumar et al. (2023) in the context of fine-tuning showed that penalizing rank collapse via spectral norms prevents the feature suppression that makes sequential learning destructive, and analogous results appear in continual learning when you treat each task transition as a fine-tuning event. The interference with compression is real but asymmetric: nuclear norm penalties hurt within-task sample efficiency measurably (roughly 10–20% more data needed to reach the same training loss), because the optimizer can't exploit the low-rank shortcuts that make individual task learning fast, but they hurt cross-task interference disproportionately less—the tradeoff is favorable when you have more than 4–5 tasks. The deeper problem is that full spectral regularization is undiscriminating: it penalizes all rank reduction equally, but not all rank reduction is harmful—compressing redundant within-task dimensions is fine and desirable, while compressing the between-task orthogonal directions is what causes fragmentation. This suggests the right target is selective spectral regularization: penalize rank reduction specifically in the subspace spanned by prior task representations, which is essentially what methods like GPCL (Gradient Projection Continual Learning variants) approximate, but doing it directly in activation space rather than gradient space is more geometrically honest. The fundamental tension this reveals is that efficient single-task learning and efficient continual learning have opposing geometric preferences—single-task learning wants to find the lowest-rank sufficient statistic for the task, while continual learning wants to keep the representation space high-rank and spread; any optimizer that serves both must explicitly schedule between these objectives rather than hoping a single regularization constant resolves the conflict.

The crossover point is surprisingly early and concrete: storing the top-k singular vectors of the activation covariance matrix per task (the standard way to represent a task's subspace) costs O(d·k) floats per task where d is the embedding dimension, and for a typical ResNet-18 layer with d=512 and k=50 retained components, that's 25,600 floats per task per layer—across 10 layers and 20 tasks, you're at ~5M floats just for subspace metadata, which at float32 is 20MB, comparable to storing 1,000–2,000 raw CIFAR images in a replay buffer that would likely do more work. GPM's own ablations (Saha et al., 2021) show that subspace quality degrades measurably after ~10 tasks because the covariance estimates from early tasks become stale as the network's earlier layers drift—the subspace you computed for task 1 at layer 3 no longer accurately reflects where task 1's representations currently live after 9 subsequent tasks have shifted that layer's weights. The metadata also compounds in a way raw data doesn't: each new task requires you to orthogonalize against all prior subspaces, an operation that costs O(k²·T) at task T, while replay buffer sampling stays O(buffer_size) regardless of task count. There's a more fundamental issue that raw data doesn't have: subspace metadata is non-revisable—once you've computed and stored the singular vectors for task 1, you can't cheaply update them when layer 3 drifts, whereas raw replay data automatically reflects the current network's behavior when you re-embed it. The practical conclusion drawn implicitly by methods like DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020) is that storing raw logits or embeddings alongside data points is more robust than storing geometric metadata precisely because the raw data can be re-processed through whatever the current network is, while frozen subspace descriptors become increasingly fictitious representations of a network state that no longer exists.

The equivalence is real and has been partially formalized: any subspace-based method that re-computes its descriptors using the current network on stored exemplars is performing replay with extra steps, and the information bottleneck is identical—what you can protect is bounded by what data you retained, not by the sophistication of the geometric machinery you apply to it. Verwimp et al. (2021) made this argument empirically in their "replay benchmark" paper, showing that well-tuned experience replay (ER) with sufficient buffer size matches or exceeds most regularization and subspace methods on standard benchmarks, and the margin grows with task count precisely because geometric methods accumulate the staleness error you described while replay doesn't. The deeper theoretical point comes from viewing both approaches as approximating the same object: the Fisher information matrix of all prior tasks, which characterizes exactly which parameter directions matter for prior performance—replay approximates this by resampling the data distribution, subspace methods approximate it by storing its eigenvectors, and both approximations degrade at the same rate as a function of how well the stored information represents the true posterior over prior tasks. What distinguishes them is not the constraint they enforce but the currency in which they pay the storage cost: subspace methods front-load the compression (lossy, fixed at capture time), while replay methods defer it (lossless until you decide buffer size, re-processable). This implies the two strategies are not distinct in kind but differ in where they place an irreducible tradeoff—and the practical implication is clarifying: there is no free geometric lunch, and methods that claim to avoid replay while achieving comparable performance are either operating in a regime where tasks are sufficiently similar that small subspaces suffice, or they are implicitly storing equivalent information in a less transparent form.

The choice is not purely engineering—there are distribution regimes where the approximations diverge in quality in provable ways. In the high input-overlap, low label-overlap regime (the classic "split" benchmark structure, e.g., Split-CIFAR where all tasks share natural image statistics but partition disjoint classes), subspace methods are provably tighter approximations of the Fisher because the Fisher's dominant eigenvectors are shared across tasks—the input covariance is similar, so a subspace captured from task 1 genuinely describes a direction that task 2's gradients also inhabit, meaning orthogonalization is geometrically meaningful rather than fictitious. Replay, conversely, becomes tighter when tasks have low input overlap but high structural similarity in label space—for instance, cross-domain continual learning (sketch→photo→clipart in DomainNet) where the Fisher eigenvectors shift dramatically between tasks because the pixel statistics are incomparable, but the semantic decision boundaries are analogous; here raw data replay re-grounds the Fisher estimate in the current feature space naturally, while subspace methods orthogonalize against directions that no longer exist in the new input manifold. There is a formalization of this in the kernel regime: Bennani et al. (2020) showed that in the NTK approximation, the Fisher overlap between tasks is directly proportional to the kernel similarity of their input distributions, which gives you a concrete diagnostic—measure inter-task kernel distance, and if it exceeds a threshold (roughly, if tasks are more than one kernel length-scale apart), replay dominates; if below, subspace methods are more parameter-efficient. The practically underappreciated case is adversarial overlap: tasks engineered to have high input similarity but maximally different gradients (like permuted MNIST variants with structured rather than random permutations), where both approximations fail badly because the Fisher is high-rank in exactly the directions both methods assume are compressible—this regime exposes that the real binding assumption both methods share is Fisher low-rankness, and when that breaks, neither strategy has a principled advantage.
